The Hand You Can't See

About 5 minutes Your browser can't read this page aloud.
TLDR
  • In zardozi, the needle works entirely underneath the stretched fabric — the karigar's hand below can't see the beadwork taking shape on top, and works purely by feel.
  • A through-hole component on a circuit board gets the same split: placed from the top, but actually bonded — soldered — from underneath, usually by a wave of molten metal the installer never watches happen.
  • Both are reserved today for the places that need real strength: the heavy, high-relief motifs on one side; the connectors and big capacitors that take a physical knock on the other.
  • Number to remember: how much metal thread a single piece can carry.

Then

The frame, and the hand below

Stretch a length of silk drum-tight across a wooden frame — an adda — and seat two or three karigars around it. On top, someone lays out the design: coiled wire called dabka, flattened wire called badla, star-shaped sequins called sitara, glass beads, pearls. Underneath, out of sight, another hand works a hooked needle up through the cloth, again and again, catching each piece and locking it in place from below — purely by feel, by the resistance of the thread, by years of practice. The person doing the actual stitching never sees the finished motif until the frame is lifted.

The name comes from Persian — zar, gold, and dozi, sewing — and the craft's roots run even deeper: gold embroidery turns up in accounts of the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, and again through the Sultanate period, long before it peaked under Mughal patronage in the 17th century, when zardozi on silk and velvet signalled wealth the way a brocade crest might.

Before any thread is laid, the motif has to get onto the cloth. A design is first sketched on tracing or butter paper and pricked through with a needle until it's a sheet of tiny holes. That sheet is laid over the fabric and dabbed with a mixture of chalk powder and kerosene, so the dust prints straight through the holes — a step called chappai. Only then is the cloth stitched onto a stiff backing cloth, the patti, and stretched onto the adda for 4 to 6 karigars to work from both sides at once.

Patronage thinned after independence, then the craft found new life in exhibitions and export markets, and in new motifs — homes, people, flora and fauna alongside the old Islamic florals, paisleys and jaalis. Lucknow zardozi has carried a Geographical Indication tag since 2013. None of it is fast work; nothing about zardozi is meant to be.

  • Step 1Tracing

    The design is pricked through tracing paper, then chalked onto the fabric — chappai.

  • Step 2Stretching

    The cloth is stitched to a backing patti and tensioned onto the wooden adda.

  • Step 3Embroidery

    Beads go on top, the hooked needle works from below — by feel, not sight.

  • Step 4Finishing

    Threads trimmed, cloth washed, dried and pressed before it's ready.

Soldered from below

That same split — work the top only, or divide the job across two sides that never see each other — is holding together the device you're reading this on.

A through-hole component puts its legs through drilled holes from the top of a circuit board, same as a sequin laid on silk. But the bond that actually makes it an electrical connection, rather than a loose piece of metal, happens underneath — usually by running the whole board, face-down, over a standing wave of molten solder. Nobody solders by eye down there. The wave just finds every leg that's poking through, the same way the hidden needle finds every bead by feel, not sight.

It's also the slower, more deliberate of the two ways to build a circuit board — which is exactly why it's reserved today for the parts that need to survive real mechanical stress: connectors you'll plug and unplug thousands of times, big capacitors, anything that takes a physical knock. Everything else on the board gets the fast treatment, placed and bonded on one side alone.

Zardozi earns its place the same way. It isn't spread across the whole garment — it's saved for where the weight and the raised relief actually matter: borders, necklines, the one motif meant to catch the light.

Try it · worked from below Everything happens in your browser

The frame, or the board, at an angle — the way a karigar actually sees it. Pick a motif and step through: placed on top first, then bonded from underneath, out of sight.

Turn either one over, and the family resemblance stops. The back of a zardozi motif is a tangle of thread floats and knots, following no order a machine could read — only the karigar's hand knows the pattern. The underside of a through-hole board is the opposite: rows of solder fillets, so uniform a machine can inspect them by eye, one bad joint standing out instantly against the rest.

That's the trade a hidden hand makes, whichever century it's working in: give up the ability to see what you're doing, and gain a kind of strength that can't be faked from the top. A needle that finds its bead by feel. A wave that finds every leg by touch. Neither one needs to watch itself work — it only needs to be underneath, at exactly the right moment.
